articles.title: Politics live: Monique Ryan ‘not bothered’ by Josh Frydenberg comeback speculation
articles.excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The release of Josh Frydenberg’s book this week has reheated speculation the former Liberal treasurer could have another go at his former s...
articles.body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The release of Josh Frydenberg’s book this week has reheated speculation the former Liberal treasurer could have another go at his former seat of Kooyong in Melbourne.

But Monique Ryan, the independent who won the seat from Frydenberg in 2022, says she’s “not bothered” by all the chatter.

She told Nine earlier this morning Frydenberg seemed more interested in being prime minister than worrying about his electorate:

double quotation markJosh does have a track record with the Kooyong community. He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change. People were unhappy with his economic management. People were very unhappy with the way that he punched down on Victoria during the Covid years …

He says he wants to be prime minister, but he doesn’t speak much about Kooyong, and that’s the part of the world that I’m most focused on.

Ryan might not be fazed but I’m sure the small (and real) “waiting for Josh Frydenberg” (WFJF) faction of the Liberal party have fingers and toes crossed for a political resurrection.

Lambie accuses Labor of ‘financial coercion’ over FoI court fight

Independent senator Jacqui Lambie is accusing the government of “financial coercion” over its push to get former senator Rex Patrick to cover the commonwealth’s legal costs over a fight in court for access to freedom of information documents.

Patrick could be on the hook for up to $150,000 to cover the government’s legal costs if he loses a fight to access requested FoI documents on the Aukus agreement. She says that will set a dangerous precedent.

Lambie says the attempt to fight the FoI requests in court follows the government being forced to drop its controversial changes to FoI legislation last year.

Lambie is proposing a bill to force the government to meet a “citizen’s reasonable legal costs if it appeals a citizen’s FoI win to the federal court from either the information commissioner or the administrative review tribunal”. She says:

double quotation markThat bill had no friends! But thanks to civil society groups and the crossbench, the government shelved the legislation in March 2026. But the governments war on our FoI laws has gone on.

Australians know the term ‘coercive control’ – what the federal Labor government is doing is financial coercion.

There will be plenty of chatter across the corridors of parliament after the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) this weekend which featured the leaders of the three main conservative parties – One Nation’s Pauline Hanson, the Liberal’s Angus Taylor and the Nationals’ Matt Canavan.

My colleague Josh Butler spent the weekend there and said the reception at the conference suggested Hanson was the preferred opposition leader.

Wondering what actually happens at one of these things? Take a look at Butler’s analysis below:

Tim Wilson feels lukewarm on Josh Frydenberg’s return to politics

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, is pretty lukewarm on a potential Josh Frydenberg return to parliament and hints the former treasurer would have to sit within the pecking order.

Wilson is pretty adamant on RN Breakfast that any political resurrection would be under the Liberals’ current leader Angus Taylor.

He speaks pretty broadly on the question, and says he has “no issue with people putting themselves forward” – it’s not exactly a warm welcome.

double quotation markI think it’s always good to have candidates who want to step up and run and make sure we pick up seats so that Angus Taylor can be prime minister of this country.

What we need is people who’ve got courage in their hearts and prepared to make the sacrifices necessary for public office. So, I have no issue with people putting themselves forward.

I encourage them to do so so they can be part of a winning team, so we can have an Angus Taylor-led government.

Host Sally Sara asks whether Wilson supports a reported idea from Frydenberg that the GST take should be increased and whether it’s helpful for the Coalition to have ex-pollies making suggestions from the sidelines.

Wilson says taxes should not be increased, but throws Frydenberg a bone:

double quotation markWell, I believe we want a better country, and that’s through a contest of ideas. But in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis, we’re not going to be increasing taxes. In fact, we want to do the complete reverse.

Mulino dodges question on whether Australia should block livestream of US execution

Daniel Mulino doesn’t want to comment when asked whether Labor would support the Greens’ call to block the livestream of a firing squad execution in the US.

Earlier this morning, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said she wrote to the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, and the communications minister, Anika Wells, to stop the live stream, and that the government should slap fines on any tech platform that showed the stream or didn’t take steps block the video later.

Mulino at first dodges the question completely and says very broadly that the government is “forward leaning” on tech safety. Obviously not satisfied with the answer, host Sally Sara tries again. Mulino replies he doesn’t want to comment on “domestic politics of any other country when it comes to matters like this”.

Sara then asks her next guest, the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, the same question. He’s a lot more forthcoming, but says it would be a challenge to block the live stream without it amounting to a “censorship ban on the internet”.

double quotation markMy basic principle is we shouldn’t be promoting that sort of violence. And so my fundamental view is yes, I think it’s enormously problematic to tolerate this type of behaviour. But the challenge is going to be: how do you do that in a way that doesn’t amount to a censorship ban on the internet?

If it’s going to be livestreamed, how are you going to do that without creating the artifice to be able to block content on the internet and create an online portal of censorship? And I don’t, the specifics of that, I’ll have to leave to others.

Labor not watering down trust tax bill, says Mulino

The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, says Labor is not watering down proposed changes to put a minimum 30% tax on discretionary trusts.

Mulino tells ABC RN Breakfast there have been changes made to the legislation since it was first announced, including carve-outs for discretionary testamentary trusts, but he’s tight-lipped on what else has been adjusted.

double quotation markWe’re not watering this down. This is a very substantial review. This is about fairness in our tax system. It’s about trying to better align the taxes that people pay when they earn income through trusts versus when they earn income from working, from providing their labour.

These are changes that have been called for by experts for decades. If we go back to major reviews in the 1970s and all the way through the Howard government, the Henry review, even the Abbott government’s review, these changes to trust taxation have been called for.

The Coalition are certainly no fans of the legislation and have called for it to be scrapped completely.

Asked about warnings from the opposition that the trust changes could harm small businesses, Mulino doesn’t say much, just that the government “has taken a number of actions when it comes to small business”.

Josh Frydenberg has literally propelled the comeback speculation himself and said he’s not closing the door to another tilt at federal politics and going for the top job, during a publicity blitz ahead of the release of his memoir.

In a lengthy interview with 60 Minutes last night he told Tracy Grimshaw the Liberal party was facing an existential threat and had to change.

Asked whether current Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, would appreciate the feedback that he’s “getting it wrong”, Frydenberg said:

double quotation markI think he’s getting that from lots of corners. People are saying that the Liberal party needs to do better.

The polls are showing that the Liberal party is at an all-time low. And so, things have to change. Because there’s something existential about the threat that I think the party now faces.

So, Grimshaw asks, does Frydenberg still want to become prime minister?

double quotation markLook, I certainly haven’t closed the door, but I don’t need to rush to a decision. The next election is 18 months away.

The release of Josh Frydenberg’s book this week has reheated speculation the former Liberal treasurer could have another go at his former seat of Kooyong in Melbourne.

But Monique Ryan, the independent who won the seat from Frydenberg in 2022, says she’s “not bothered” by all the chatter.

She told Nine earlier this morning Frydenberg seemed more interested in being prime minister than worrying about his electorate:

double quotation markJosh does have a track record with the Kooyong community. He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change. People were unhappy with his economic management. People were very unhappy with the way that he punched down on Victoria during the Covid years …

He says he wants to be prime minister, but he doesn’t speak much about Kooyong, and that’s the part of the world that I’m most focused on.

Ryan might not be fazed but I’m sure the small (and real) “waiting for Josh Frydenberg” (WFJF) faction of the Liberal party have fingers and toes crossed for a political resurrection.

More states to sign on to AusAlert system ahead of ‘disaster season’, minister says

Kristy McBain, the emergency management minister, is doing the media rounds, to talk ahead of what could be a brutal and damaging summer season in Australia.

On Monday a total fire ban was declared across both the Greater Sydney and Greater Hunter regions as the temperature was forecast to climb into the 30s.

You might remember a couple of months ago there was a national test of the AusAlert system, where all compatible phones sounded an alarm and displayed a test message.

McBain tells ABC News Breakfast just two states have so far signed on to the system, but more will be going through that process in the coming weeks “before we hit disaster season proper”.

double quotation markThat will get much better protection for communities who are experiencing disaster, as I said. Near real-time message not [reliant] on any one telco provider is a real gamechanger for emergency management.

Labor frontbencher Kristy McBain says the Reserve Bank should go a step further than its card surcharge ban, and ban charging at the point of sale for small businesses.

The government has copped a bit of flack from the card surcharge ban, which was costing consumers $1.6bn a year, with som small businesses raising the price of their goods in response.

McBain tells Seven’s Sunrise that the government isn’t in charge of these decisions – the Reserve Bank is – but small businesses shouldn’t have to keep paying fees to card networks or banks to accept those card and digital payments.

double quotation markThese banks are making billions of dollars in profits every year and small businesses are already paying account-keeping fees and a range of other fees directly to their banks.

I’d like to see the RBA actually take that next step and say there is no charging for those point of sale machines.

Big tech, health and education on the parliamentary agenda

Good morning, Krishani Dhanji with you here on our politics blog to cover another busy sitting week.

Time is quickly running out for the government who have a few key pieces of legislation they want to pass with only three joint sitting weeks left in the year and one Senate-only sitting week.

As my colleague Tom McIlroy has brought you this morning, Labor’s digital duty of care bill will be in the spotlight, with the Greens putting themselves at the negotiation table. They want bigger fines – a share of global revenue – for tech platforms that do the wrong thing.

Health and education are also on the legislative agenda: the government’s plan to reduce private health insurance rebates for over-65s isn’t loved (or at all liked, really) by the Coalition or the Greens so they’ll need to find a way around that. But the opposition and Greens are more supportive of a bill to change university funding, which guarantees spots for students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, regional, rural and First Nations families (though expect lots of amendments).

NSW government moves to challenge One Nation to cost promises

The NSW government will seek to amend legislation to give One Nation access to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office in a bid to challenge the populist party to cost their promises.

In a statement, the Minns government said it was clear the March 2027 election would see three parties competing to form government – and the legislation only contemplates a Labor v Coalition contest.

The treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, said he was “looking forward” to seeing One Nation’s ideas.

double quotation markBut right now, voters will only get advice from the independent PBO on the costs of the Coalition and Labor’s policies. They should get that same advice about One Nation’s policies.

One Nation has made no secret of how much they admire American and Argentinian-style wage policies, healthcare policies and cuts to the public service.

No doubt they will want to import these ideas into NSW, but voters deserve to have independent advice about what they mean for them.

The opposition says reports the FlyDubai pilot involved in a thwarted hijacking was radicalised while studying in Australia are “deeply disturbing”.

At the weekend, the attorney-general of the United Arab Emirates said that pilot Hamad Saif al-Shamsi underwent a “drift towards extremism and terrorism” while studying in Melbourne.

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said there could be no place for hate preachers or anyone advocating terror or violence in the country.

double quotation markThat is why the Coalition will tighten visa laws to keep those who preach hatred out of Australia and deport non-citizens who promote violent extremism.

Extremism has no place in Australia. We need to detect it early, confront it wherever it emerges and give our police and security agencies the resources they need to keep Australians safe.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said the man was radicalised online, as extremist groups target young people, particularly men. He said the government wanted to properly screen people at the border and in online settings.

Al-Shamsi received a student visa for study in Australia in 2014. He left in 2017 and his visa was cancelled two years later.

The Greens are pushing for the Albanese government to ensure the live streaming of a firing squad execution in the US is not able to be viewed in Australia.

Last week, the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, said the public would be able to watch the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan on 3 December.

The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has written to the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, and the communications minister, Anika Wells, seeking assurance it won’t be shown in Australia.

Hanson-Young suggested large fines could apply for digital platforms if they showed the stream or did not take steps to block the video at a later date.

double quotation markI think this is incredibly shocking and barbaric, and Australians don’t want this on our screens.

Good morning and welcome to Monday’s politics coverage.

Krishani Dhanji will be with you shortly.

articles.title: El-Sayed asked if he believes America is 'ready for a Muslim president' ahead of Senate race
articles.excerpt:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was asked by "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker whether America is ready to elect a Muslim president.

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-S...
articles.body_text:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was asked by "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker whether America is ready to elect a Muslim president.

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed remarked on whether he would consider running for president of the United States, during an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday.

Host Kristen Welker closed her interview asking El-Sayed whether he believed America was "ready" to elect a Muslim candidate for president.

"That's not a question I'm asking," El-Sayed answered. "I think Michigan is ready for a Muslim senator."

MICHIGAN DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED JABS CNN GIVING HIM 'NON-CONSENSUAL COLONOSCOPY' IN RECENT INTERVIEWS

U.S. Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan Abdul El-Sayed told "Meet the Press" that he has no interest in running for president. (Jeff Kowalsky / AFP via Getty Images)

Welker repeated the question, but El-Sayed continued to say the question was "irrelevant" and that Michigan was ready for a Muslim senator.

"Okay, but you don't rule out the possibility that—?" Welker asked.

"I have no intention of ever running for president. That is not a thing I've ever wanted to do," El-Sayed said.

EL-SAYED TAUNTS TRUMP, CLAIMS HE'S GOING TO MAKE HIM 'MAIN CHARACTER OF THE MIDTERMS'

He continued, "I want to be a really great senator for my state. You know, someday, somewhere, somebody down the line decides to run, that would have been a really amazing thing to see how big America really is. But for right now, I really want to be the next senator from Michigan. That's what I’d like to be for a long time to come. I'm looking forward to serving out the next six years. I'm honored to get to do this. And look, America is a big place, and America has this incredible way of reminding us how big she really is. And that starts in Michigan."

During the interview, Welker also asked another question about a presidential run while referencing a reported comment made by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., where she remarked, "If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere."

Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, has repeatedly denied being connected to the Muslim Brotherhood. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL

"If you lose Michigan, does that mean that a progressive like AOC can't win the White House in 2028?" Welker said.

"Look, this is one seat in Michigan that has a lot more to do with our local issues in Michigan than it has to do with a national referendum," El-Sayed said.

Fox News Digital reached out to NBC and El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

El-Sayed's interview came after his Thursday debate with GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers in which Rogers brought up alleged ties between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist organization.

El-Sayed has repeatedly denied these ties. He also rejected the premise when asked by Welker.

Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers faced off against each other in a recent debate. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images; Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"No," he said, before claiming the allegation was based in Islamophobia.

"It's truly shameful, but he has no ideas, he doesn't actually care about solving problems," El-Sayed said of Rogers.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Media Research Center President David Bozell criticized what he considered Welker's eagerness to consider El-Sayed a presidential candidate.

"NBC took one look at Abdul El-Sayed and started planning the presidential library. Never mind Hasan Piker. Never mind Michigan. Meet the Press skipped the vetting and went straight to measuring El-Sayed’s Oval Office drapes," Bozell said.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Aaron Rodgers defies Father Time with another three-touchdown performance in Steelers’ win
articles.excerpt:
Tom Rinaldi looks back at the life and legacy of NFL legend Mike Ditka, reflecting on his impact on the game and the lasting mark he left on generations of football fans.

I thought Aaron Rodgers was ...
articles.body_text:
Tom Rinaldi looks back at the life and legacy of NFL legend Mike Ditka, reflecting on his impact on the game and the lasting mark he left on generations of football fans.

I thought Aaron Rodgers was cooked coming into the 2026 season, and his performances in the first two weeks did little to change my mind.

In my Week 2 takeaways column, I described him as "an old quarterback whose career probably should have ended three years ago."

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Yeah, so, that assessment could use an update.

Aaron Rodgers threw three touchdowns as the Steelers beat the Colts 34-22, surpassing Peyton Manning for third in career touchdown passes, including the postseason. (Getty Images)

The 42-year-old threw three touchdown passes Sunday as the Pittsburgh Steelers beat the Indianapolis Colts, 34-22, to improve to 3-2. Rodgers finished with 235 passing yards and has now thrown three touchdowns in three consecutive games.

'WHAT THE F--K, CALL IT!': AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY CURSE AT EACH OTHER DURING HOT MIC MOMENT

Over that stretch, he's passed for 826 yards and nine touchdowns. That's pretty good production for anyone, let alone a quarterback who is likely playing in his final NFL season.

For comparison, Rodgers had more turnovers (2) than touchdown passes (1) in the first two games.

Now, he's still averaging one turnover per game after throwing three interceptions in the past three games, so he has to clean that up.

He didn’t turn the ball over Sunday, though, showing he's still got some football left in that 42-year-old right arm.

The encouraging part for Pittsburgh is that Rodgers is giving the offense something to build on each week.

Sunday's opening possession went backward, costing the Steelers 15 yards before they punted. But Rodgers responded quickly. On Pittsburgh's next possession, he got the ball to Jaylen Warren just before taking a hit from defensive tackle Grover Stewart, and Warren turned the short completion into an 80-yard touchdown.

Aaron Rodgers and Jaylen Warren of the Pittsburgh Steelers celebrate after scoring a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts at Acrisure Stadium. (Getty Images)

Rodgers went on to complete his first 11 passes and didn't have an incompletion until midway through the second quarter.

Of course, Warren deserves plenty of credit for making his quarterback's numbers look better. He finished with 188 yards from scrimmage and added a 50-yard touchdown run to go with the long receiving score. That's a pretty productive afternoon.

JASON KELCE’S EAGLES-JAGUARS BROADCAST SHOWS WHY NFL BOOTHS COULD USE MORE OFFENSIVE LINEMEN

But Rodgers also delivered when Pittsburgh needed to put some distance between itself and Indianapolis.

With the Steelers leading 24-22 in the fourth quarter, Rodgers found Pat Freiermuth for a 17-yard touchdown on third-and-6. It was Freiermuth's second touchdown catch of the afternoon and basically locked up the victory.

There were a couple of historical accomplishments mixed in, too.

The touchdown pass to Warren moved Rodgers ahead of Peyton Manning for third in career touchdown passes, including the postseason. Only Tom Brady and Drew Brees remain ahead of him.

DRE GREENLAW'S SEAN PAYTON BEEF EXPOSES ANOTHER SIDE OF THE NFL'S MOST OVERRATED HEAD COACH

The victory also gave Rodgers 166 regular-season wins as a starting quarterback, moving him past Ben Roethlisberger into fifth place all time. Passing a Steelers legend while wearing a Steelers uniform is a nice bonus.

The career accomplishments are impressive, obviously. But Steelers fans have a more immediate interest in whether Rodgers can keep playing like this.

Aaron Rodgers threw three touchdown passes as the Pittsburgh Steelers beat the Indianapolis Colts 34-22. The 42-year-old has now thrown nine TDs in his past three games. (Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Pittsburgh needs an offense that can take advantage when its defense gets stops, finish drives with touchdowns and deliver a big play when a game gets uncomfortable. Rodgers and Warren gave the Steelers all of that against Indianapolis.

There's still plenty of season left, and three good games don't settle every question about this team. They're also in the very competitive AFC North, where all four teams have three wins already.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The upcoming schedule provides an opportunity for Rodgers and the Steelers to keep rolling. Pittsburgh plays at Tampa Bay in Week 6 and then faces New Orleans in Paris. The Buccaneers and Saints are a combined 2-8.

After that comes a pair of crucial division games against the Browns and Bengals with a bye week in between. It remains to be seen if Rodgers can keep up this level of production as the season wears on.

But after throwing nine touchdown passes in three games? Yeah, I probably buried Rodgers a little too soon.

articles.title: Trump Russia deal could fuel Putin's war, ex-NATO commander warns as Zelenskyy says 'nyet'
articles.excerpt:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns Russia will use oil revenue to finance attacks while buying time at the negotiating table.

President Donald Trump's efforts to reach a diesel agreement with Russia...
articles.body_text:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns Russia will use oil revenue to finance attacks while buying time at the negotiating table.

President Donald Trump's efforts to reach a diesel agreement with Russia could provide Russian President Vladimir Putin with fresh revenue to fund his war against Ukraine while allowing Moscow to buy time through negotiations it has little intention of honoring, a former NATO commander warned Sunday.

Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO supreme allied commander Europe and head of U.S. European Command, told Fox News Digital that Washington also risks undermining Ukraine's war effort by striking a deal with what he called "the enemy."

"And so we are cutting a deal with the enemy," Breedlove said, warning that "all of this money will go into fueling Mr. Putin's continued attacks in Ukraine."

The Russian government said Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports with immediate effect, following the new agreement between Putin and Trump for Russia to supply the U.S. and global markets, Reuters reported.

As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Trump's package calls for the release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace," followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another 1 million tonnes afterward.

KATIE ZACHARIA HITS GROUND RUNNING, PROMISES TRUMP DIESEL DEAL DELIVERS CHEAPER GAS FOR AMERICANS

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a briefing in Kyiv, Ukraine, Thursday, April 17, 2025. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

The diesel agreement preceded Trump's announcement Sunday of what he called an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, with the president saying both sides had agreed to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, indicated that Ukraine had not been informed of a finalized ceasefire agreement but expressed willingness to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow reciprocated. He also accused Putin of repeatedly rejecting peace proposals and continuing strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

"Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them – 'nyet,'" Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"We do hope that he will finally say something to America, Ukraine, and the entire world that will lead to a real and dignified peace," he added.

Zelenskyy also said Russian forces had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission facilities over the past week, along with 17 strikes targeting gas and oil infrastructure.

He said the attacks had killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 over the past week.

Trump's "energy ceasefire" announcement followed tension between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, a component of Ukraine's strategy to weaken Moscow's ability to finance its military campaign.

UKRAINE TARGETS RUSSIA WITH OVER 1,000 DRONES, KILLING 2 AS MOSCOW HOLDS LAST DAY OF ELECTIONS

A view of Russian President Vladimir Putin in front of the Kremlin. (Reuters/Tom Szlukovenyi | Photo by Contributor/Getty Images | Fox News Digital)

Breedlove argued that Russia and Ukraine are pursuing different objectives, accusing Moscow of targeting Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure while describing Kyiv's attacks on Russian energy facilities as an effort to disrupt the revenue sustaining Putin's war.

"Russia is carrying on a campaign of what we call counter value. In other words, Russia is attacking the Ukrainian people and trying to force their society to separate themselves from their president, President Zelenskyy," Breedlove said.

Breedlove also predicted Washington would pressure Zelenskyy to suspend attacks on Russia's oil industry despite their strategic importance.

"What I expect will happen is the United States will force or try to force Zelenskyy to stop bombing the petrochemical business in Russia," he said.

TRUMP'S DIESEL IDEA COULD HAVE UNLEASHED A PROBLEM AMERICANS NEVER SAW COMING

Overnight, Russia launched its largest aerial assault on Ukraine since the war started as fires burned in Kyiv on May 25, 2025. (Reuters/Gleb Garanich)

Trump has vehemently criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, arguing that they are disrupting global diesel supplies and driving up costs for American farmers and ranchers.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the administration's efforts to increase diesel supplies.

"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have," Bessent said Sunday on Fox News. "This is good for the American people, bringing these diesel prices down," he said of the new deal.

Separately, appearing on ABC News' "This Week," Zelenskyy offered to organize Ukrainian elections if Putin agreed to a reciprocal 60-day ceasefire, although holding a vote would face legal and logistical obstacles under Ukraine's martial law.

Breedlove also expressed deep skepticism that Putin would honor any such ceasefire, citing what he described as a pattern of Russian attacks following negotiations with Trump. "Russia has never kept a promise to this president in this war," Breedlove said.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. The two leaders are meeting for peace talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine. (Getty Images/ Andrew Harnik)

"He's never changed his expectations, and he's never delivered on his promises. Three out of four of the big cases, the very next day or that same night after the president and Mr. Putin talked, Mr. Putin launched huge attacks in Ukraine," Breedlove continued.

Breedlove also called for a tougher U.S. response.

"We now need an administration that leads from power. We say all the time, 'strength through power,' but when it comes to Russia, our demonstrated position is continued conflict through weakness," Breedlove warned.

"He started this war. This war is to benefit Russia, and this war is to keep Mr. Putin in power. And our administration needs to tell him to stop."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and American friend on Mexico surfing trip
articles.excerpt:
Three bodies have been discovered in a Mexican tourist area where an American and two Australians are missing. CREDIT: Reuters

Three men have been convicted in the brutal killings of two Australian b...
articles.body_text:
Three bodies have been discovered in a Mexican tourist area where an American and two Australians are missing. CREDIT: Reuters

Three men have been convicted in the brutal killings of two Australian brothers and their American friend, whose disappearance on a Mexico surf trip sparked an international search before their bodies were found dumped in a well.

A judge in Ensenada on Friday found Jesús Gerardo García, known as "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N," and Ángel Jesús "N," guilty of murdering Callum and Jake Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, in Baja, California, in April 2024, The Associated Press reported.

The men were also convicted of armed robbery and armed carjacking. Judge Raúl Hernández is scheduled to announce their sentences Oct. 16, with the Baja California State Attorney General’s Office seeking 210 years in prison for each defendant, according to the AP.

MINNESOTA FATHER CONVICTED OF KILLING TEENAGE SON WHOSE REMAINS WERE FOUND IN LANDFILL

Martin and Debra Robinson, parents of murdered Australian surfers Callum and Jake Robinson, speak to reporters. Three men were convicted in the brothers’ killings and the murder of their American friend Carter Rhoad. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

The verdicts followed a month-long trial that included testimony about one victim pleading for his life before the killings.

García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, testified that he told her he approached the surfers’ tent carrying a 9mm pistol, the AP reported. The men threw their belongings toward him in an effort to stop the attack, and one begged to be spared, she said.

AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANT'S ALLEGED KILLERS TIED TO GANG ACCUSED OF PREYING ON TOURISTS: OFFICIALS

According to her testimony, García ignored the plea.

The friends had traveled to Baja, California, to surf and were reported missing after arriving in Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada. Their bodies were discovered in a well May 3, 2024.

MEXICAN SPORTS JOURNALIST ROBBED AT GUNPOINT DURING LIVE REPORT

Demonstrators march in Ensenada, Mexico, after Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad were killed during a 2024 surfing trip. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

Authorities initially said the men were killed after confronting thieves who wanted the tires from their pickup truck.

Chief state prosecutor María Elena Andrade Ramírez said at the time that investigators believed the thieves spotted the truck and tents, then encountered resistance from the surfers during the attempted theft.

García allegedly told his girlfriend he had done something to "three gringos" before admitting, "I killed them," according to the BBC’s account of a May 2024 court hearing.

She also said he showed her a vehicle fitted with tires allegedly stolen from the victims’ truck.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

Debra and Martin Robinson, parents of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, leave the courthouse after the trial of the men accused of murdering the brothers and an American friend, in Ensenada, Mexico, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

Silva Raya was found with one victim’s cellphone. Prosecutors said she met the surfers April 27, 2024, and urged one of her companions to rob them, the AP reported.

She pleaded guilty to aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence and was sentenced to 20 years in prison in November 2025. García and the other two men went to trial.

JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER

The guilty verdicts brought a measure of relief to the Robinson family more than two years after the brothers’ deaths.

Their father, Martin Robinson, described the decision as a significant moment in the family’s painful pursuit of justice, according to the AP. He said the outcome could not undo their loss but offered a step toward justice as they continued honoring the three men.

MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO 2023 KILLING OF LAUREN HEIKE ON PHOENIX HIKING TRAIL

Martin and Debra Robinson, whose sons Callum and Jake were killed on a surfing trip in Mexico, walk together outside a building. The brothers and their American friend Carter Rhoad were found dead in a well in May 2024. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

The brothers’ mother, Debra Robinson, spoke about their love of surfing during a tribute on a San Diego beach shortly after their bodies were found.

"Our hearts are broken, and the world has become a darker place for us," she said at the time. "They were young men enjoying their passion of surfing together."

She recalled that Jake, a doctor, sought work at hospitals near surfing beaches and urged others to honor her sons by embracing life.

"Live bigger, shine brighter, and love harder in their memory," she said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent
articles.excerpt:
Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.

The US president insisted that it was "...
articles.body_text:
Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.

The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.

The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.

The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.

That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.

Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?

Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".

"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.

The BBC has asked the White House for further details.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.

Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

"All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.

For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.

Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".

The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.

Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 August

Earlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.

The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.

Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports.

"Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".

Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.

On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.

The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.

The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.

Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.

Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.

Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.

One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.

'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin

Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge

articles.title: Ben Affleck says political 'hypocrisy, corruption and failure' left him 'disillusioned'
articles.excerpt:
Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson discusses how AI may impact Hollywood productions on ‘Fox & Friends.’

Ben Affleck has no interest in running for public office.

The "Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice" star...
articles.body_text:
Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson discusses how AI may impact Hollywood productions on ‘Fox & Friends.’

Ben Affleck has no interest in running for public office.

The "Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice" star told Variety that trying to become a politician sounds "terrible" and "tawdry" to him.

"I just think that’s enormously — I don’t know, man, that seems terrible," Affleck told the outlet while promoting a new movie in which he plays a candidate for L.A. mayor. "There’s a reason why political stories are often chosen as parables for moral compromise. You really get thrust up into the contrast between the ideal version of us and how we should be in our lives and the way it is."

BEN AFFLECK DIRECTS, STARS IN NETFLIX KIDNAPPING THRILLER 'ANIMALS' COMING THIS OCTOBER

Ben Affleck said he has no interest in running for public office. (Getty Images)

The 54-year-old called politics a "very depressing world, in my opinion. Tawdry. And that has no appeal to me."

He also declined to tell the outlet who he was backing for mayor in Los Angeles this November.

"I haven’t thought about being asked that. I don’t know if, given this movie, my endorsement harms or helps anybody," he admitted. "I should stay agnostic, at least until the movie comes out."

Affleck told Good Morning America on Wednesday that he believes the "collective bar for politics because of the way the political world has sort of evolved has gotten so low that there’s this kind of like, you know, people are just sort of looking for like just ‘Somebody shoot me straight.’’"

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

He added that there’s a sense in the country, whether you’re a Democrat or a Republican that "we’re not doing a very good job. We have a system that’s kind of failing us."

Playing a man running for mayor taught him: "This is not all that much fun. And it would be a hard way — you’re just raising money all the time."

NETFLIX DROPS FULL TRAILER FOR BEN AFFLECK'S 'ANIMALS' AND EXPECTATIONS ARE ALREADY SOARING

Ben Affleck plays a man running for mayor of Los Angeles in "Animals." (Getty Images)

He said that he and the man playing his campaign manager in the movie decided one day to take campaign shirts and hats with the name of his character, go out in L.A. and claim he was running for mayor.

When he told people he was running as his character, Affleck said voters would ask for a selfie, they seemed interested and "people would launch into their whole thing and I was like ‘If I’m not careful, I’m going to win this.'"

MICHAEL RAPAPORT DOUBLES DOWN ON 2029 NYC MAYORAL RUN, VOWS 'STREET FIGHT' AGAINST ZOHRAN MAMDANI

"Do not vote for me for mayor!" he joked to the camera.

BILL MAHER REVEALS BEN AFFLECK REFUSED ‘REAL TIME’ RETURN AFTER STORMY APPEARANCE IN 2014 DEBATING ISLAM

Affleck called holding office an "awful job" in an interview with USA Today via The Sacramento Bee this week, adding that he’s "so disillusioned with the system and with politics and politicians, and the way it works."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

When told his campaign ad in the movie was good, he answered, "I'd be flattered, except I think there's such a low bar in politics these days."

Affleck explained that his movie "Animals" is about the moral compromises people make.

Ben Affleck supports then-candidate Barack Obama at an event in 2006. (WireImage)

"The extremely effective nature of when a person individually has something to lose is when they're most apt to make compromises," he says. "Are we just kind of self-seeking animals who, in retrospect, build stories to rationalize where we are and what we've done? And there's another part of us, our sort of higher selves, which says, 'Well, I'm going to adhere this moral code even if there's a cost to me.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The actor has been politically active in the past, campaigning for candidates from former Vice President Al Gore to former President Barack Obama.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

But he said he’s now "averse" to the idea because he’s seen so much "hypocrisy, corruption and failure."

"The way it's constructed now is so geared around money, sound bites, cruelties and gotchas, and little snarky things that really have nothing to do with people's lives whatsoever," he said. "And increasingly, it's easier to get votes appealing to the worst in people than it is appealing to the best in them. If you're telling a story about kind of morality and compromise, there are lots of pressures that are constantly asking you to sacrifice your principles."

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
articles.excerpt:
File photo of gold prospectors in northern Sudan

At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says.

Em...
articles.body_text:
File photo of gold prospectors in northern Sudan

At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says.

Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday.

Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented.

Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border.

Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region.

"The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes."

It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise.

The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured.

Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote.

The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers.

Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.

At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens.

Gold lies at the core of the border tensions.

Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders.

Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels.

Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment.

Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups.

This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market.

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

articles.title: Quiet part out loud: Anti-Israel mobs want one state called 'Palestine,' erasing Israel
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Digital spoke with three figures at a pro-Palestinian demonstration in Washington, D.C., asking each to lay out their vision for the future for Israelis and Palestinians.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Digital spoke with three figures at a pro-Palestinian demonstration in Washington, D.C., asking each to lay out their vision for the future for Israelis and Palestinians.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — This weekend, millions of anti-Israel activists marched through the streets of cities in coordinated actions from America's capital to London, Paris, Madrid and Kuala Lumpar, Malaysia, chanting the familiar refrains of "Free, free Palestine" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free."

But for the first time, communicated frankly in exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, three anti-Israel leaders acknowledged the goal: one state called "Palestine" encompassing modern-day Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, with a Palestinian "right of return" to the new country and equal political, voting and citizenship rights for Palestinians alongside Jews currently living in Israel.

Most significantly, in the political vision they described, Israel would legally cease to exist as a separate Jewish nation-state and Jews would be quickly overwhelmed demographically.

INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION'

Protestors march at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

The current population of Israel is about 10 million, including about 7.8 million Jews, 2 million Palestinian Arabs (including Palestinians and most of them Muslim), and 200,000 people from other communities. There are another estimated 10.2 million Jews worldwide.

There are about 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and about 8 million Palestinians in the diaspora, totaling about 13.5 million.

The candor of the anti-Israel leaders lays bare the political conclusion of an argument that activists have spent years advancing on the streets, through sympathetic media outlets and in legal forums: that Israel is a "settler colonial" state practicing "apartheid" and "genocide," and therefore should not continue to exist in its current form as a Jewish state. Israeli leaders have fiercely rejected those allegations, disputing accusations of "genocide" and "apartheid" and maintaining that Israel is the nation-state of the Jewish people with equal civil and political rights for citizens that include Jews, Christians and Muslims.

Advocates for Israel note that the nation's critics rarely apply the same historical lens of human-rights analysis to Arab and Muslim-majority states, many of which emerged from the collapse of empires, wars and population upheavals that displaced millions, including Jews expelled from their countries, today often restricting political, religious and minority rights.

NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA

In Chicago, Hatem Abudayyeh, the Palestinian-American founder of the U.S. Palestinian Community Network and a Muslim, said the new nation would be "one democratic secular state of Palestine." Jewish Israeli-born community leader Miko Peled, founder of the Palestine House in Washington, D.C., said "the proper name would be Palestine." And Maryland congressional candidate Sam Husseini, a Palestinian-American Christian, floated another name for the vision of the one state: "1948," marking the year Israel declared independence and Palestinians commemorate as the "Nakba," or catastrophe, but he said even Israeli Jews would one day accept another name: "Palestine."

Their answers provide a striking interpretation from inside a movement where activists have traditionally danced around their demands with euphemisms about "liberation" and media outlets have obscured their answers even when they have been transparent.

On Washington, D.C.'s First Avenue SE, Fox News Digital asked Olivia DiNucci, local coordinator for CodePink, a far-left nonprofit, what her group sees as a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In her work for CodePink, DiNucci disrupts hearings, restaurant meals and town halls to shout at lawmakers and policymakers who support the state of Israel.

Olivia DiNucci, D.C. coordinator at CodePink, marches at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA

"Palestinians in Palestine will decide, DiNucci said.

Asked if "Palestine" includes modern day Israel, she spun around and walked away. Later, she posted a message on social media, saying she was asked "gotcha questions."

This weekend, protesters signaled their position with certainty, explicitly rejecting the two-state solution that has dominated international diplomacy for decades.

In New York City, the Party for Socialism and Liberation circulated video of protesters marching through the streets chanting: "1-2-3-4. Occupation no more. 5-6-7-8. Israel is a terrorist state."

ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS

Then came the point: "We don't want no two state!"

In London, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign promoted a 15-second video of a woman with a megaphone shouting: "There is only one state!"

"Say it loud, say it clear!" she continued. "Palestine, you make us proud!"

Back in Washington, D.C., protesters carried signs declaring, "LAND YOU HAVE 2 KILL FOR IS NOT YOURS," a message that challenged Israel's claim to the land itself, while a banner proclaiming, "THE FIGHT FOR LIBERATION IS OURS," framed the struggle as one for the territory. The demonstrators yesterday didn't address the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, but many have called them justified.

ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'

Protestors march at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

The one-state demand is being amplified within a powerful protest infrastructure. The broader "red-green" alliance brings socialist and communist groups together on the streets with Palestinian and Muslim activist organizations, while organizations including the Democratic Socialists of America and nonprofits in the network funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon living in Shanghai, help organize, promote and amplify anti-Israel demonstrations.

Singham, has poured $278 million into a pro-communist network, including CodePink, the People's Forum, the Party for Socialism and Liberation, BreakThrough News and the ANSWER Coalition, which have become major organizing, media and logistical hubs for the protest movement. The result is a powerful infrastructure amplifying slogans such as "Free Palestine" and "from the river to the sea," even when the organizations and activists doing the amplifying don't themselves explicitly spell out the one-state political vision described to Fox News Digital.

From Chicago, Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital that the U.S. Palestinian Community Network advocates for one democratic state across the territory that today encompasses Israel, the West Bank and Gaza.

"Our points of unity, from the very beginning of our existence, included one democratic secular state of Palestine," he said.

"And for decades and decades, we've been saying that...the only true solution that can bring peace and justice to all that live there is ... one democratic state," which includes the West Bank, Gaza and "1948 Palestinian territories," a term used to describe the land that Israel claimed as a nation in 1948.

This can only happen, he said, if "the racist system of Zionism is dismantled."

The ADL, a leading Jewish organization based in New York, describes Zionism as a "movement for the self-determination and statehood for the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland, the land of Israel."

Women at an anti-Israel rally on Oct. 9, 2026, in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, hold placards reading messages created by the leaders of the Global Alliance for Palestine for protests around the country. The messages read "Humanity Is Not a Crime," "Let Gaza Live" and "Stop the Genocide War." (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)

Abudayyeh said the new state would include a "right of return" for Palestinian refugees and their descendants. "Our points of unity from day one included the right of return," he said.

Activists from a U.S.-based network of groups called "Al-Awda: The Palestine Right to Return Coalition" joined the protest in Los Angeles and posted a message online: "OUR PEOPLE WILL RETURN, PALESTINE WILL BE FREE!

"If all of our refugees, who have the internationally recognized right to return to Palestine, are able to return, and the system, the racist system is dismantled, then all the people there can live in peace and justice," Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital. "That's our position. It's always been our position. We're not going to abandon the five to seven million refugees that we have."

Marchers protest against Israel on Oct. 10, 2026 (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

"They have the right to go back to the homes and lands in which they were exiled," he explained.

Abudayyeh said that wouldn't mean removing the people – most of them Jewish – living in Israel.

"It doesn't mean that we're going to kick people out," he said. "It just means that these folks have an internationally recognized right, and you will never get peace and justice there unless you uphold that right."

"I believe, very clearly, USPCN believes very clearly that there can be peace and justice as long as that system, that racist system of Zionism is dismantled," Abudayyeh said. "That's the essence of it."

Abudayyeh compared the Palestinian movement's objective to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa. "And we're getting close to having international consensus today on the question of Israel and Zionism, where Israel doesnt have the "right to exist as a racist, Zionist, apartheid, white supremacist state."

"That's what we say," he continued. "We're adamant about that. We're clear about it. Unabashed."

Fox News Digital asked Abudayyeh whether "Palestine" includes modern-day Israel when protest leaders and activists chant "Palestine will be free" or "Free, free Palestine."

"The majority of the majority of the people, especially in the past period, have moved to that conclusion," Abudayyeh said.

Husseini, a Palestinian-American journalist running for Congress in Maryland's 4th Congressional District, offered a similar one-state vision and an unusual proposal for what the country might be called.

Standing on First Avenue SE, between the U.S. Supreme Court and the U.S. Capitol, Husseini told Fox News Digital that his long-term vision is "one person, one vote," coupled with a Palestinian right of return.

"Ultimately, long-term, I that it should be one person, one vote," Husseini said.

"Why aren't they allowed back into their homes? So I think that they should," he said of Palestinian refugees. "I mean, that includes myself. I don't know that I would actually move back there, but as a descendant of a Palestinian who was forcibly displaced, I should have that right or compensation."

Husseini offered another possibility for the country's name.

"I've often thought of a novel proposal because people get hung up on the names. Are they going to call it Israel or are they going call it Palestine?" Husseini said.

"I've toyed with the idea of calling it 1948, having a country with a number signifying the year of this cataclysm, which should be the last gasp of imperialism."

If the new state is called Palestine, Husseini said, "I think a lot of Jews, when they think about it, will say, so long as they have equal rights and all are protected, will adopt the term Palestine."

Standing on Pennsylvania Avenue SE, the roar of the demonstrators getting closer as they marched from the U.S. Capitol to talks at the Palestine House of Freedom, Miko Peled, an Israeli-born Jewish activist, was equally blunt about what a "Free Palestine" means to him.

"Well, our vision, our mission, and our vision is to educate people to see that a free Palestine, which means a post-Zionist, post-apartheid Palestine with equal rights and the right of the Palestinians to return, is the best vision that will benefit everybody who lives there currently, which means Israelis and Palestinians," he said.

Organizers from a coalition, Global Action for Palestine, share a map "Global Day of Action" events for 2026. (Global Alliance for Palestine)

Asked whether that meant one state, he answered yes.

"It's already one state, it's just an apartheid state," Peled said.

"So that's our vision, to create a real democracy, free Palestine, with equal rights."

Fox News Digital asked what that country would be called.

"Well, historically the country was called Palestine for thousands of years and so it should be called Palestine," Peled said. "Israel is a new name. They renamed the country 78 years ago, so the proper name would be Palestine."

For Peled, the familiar protest demand "Free Palestine" has a literal political meaning: One state with the new name "Palestine."

Asra Nomani is senior editor of investigations at Fox News Digital. She is a former reporter at the Wall Street Journal, where she covered stories related to money, politics and society. She is the author of "Woke Army: The Red-Green Alliance That Is Undermining America’s Freedom." She can be reached at asra.nomani@fox.com and on X at @asranomani.

articles.title: Mystery team in Marvin Harrison trade steps forward, as Texans DeMeco Ryans confirms reunion with CJ Stroud

NFL Training Camp continues, and Danny Parkins asks if C.J. Stroud is good enough to lead the Houston Texans, whether or not the Green Bay Packers offense can carry the team until Micah Parsons returns, and if the Dallas Cowboys’ offense can make them Super Bowl Contenders.

The Houston Texans beat the Tennessee Titans on Sunday for their first victory of the season, but that's not the reason coach DeMeco Ryans left his postgame news conference with a big laugh and smile.

He was asked if the Texans are indeed one of the teams interested in trading for Arizona Cardinals receiver Marvin Harrison.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

And since he was already in a good mood, Ryans made it official.

"You guys want to know, huh," Ryans said between chuckles. "Yes, alright, we traded for Marvin Harrison.

An NFL source told OutKick the Texans are sending a second and sixth-round pick to the Arizona Cardinals in exchange for Harrison and a seventh-round pick.

The Texans were one of multiple teams that talked to the Cardinals about the former first-round wide receiver as a trade target in recent days, as OutKick reported on Saturday.

Marvin Harrison Jr. (18) of the Arizona Cardinals rushes against the Dallas Cowboys during the third quarter in the game at AT&T Stadium on Nov. 03, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Sam Hodde/Getty Images)

But the lure for the Texans was tied to the fact Harrison played with quarterback C.J. Stroud at Ohio State — a combination that made both top-four draft picks in back-to-back years, 2023 and 2024.

Plus, the Texans have need on the outside because, other than Nico Collins, they have had difficulty finding a playmaker on the perimeter.

CURSED: ALL FOUR OF THE ARIZONA CARDINALS FIRST FOUR DRAFT PICKS ARE INJURED, WITH TWO OUT FOR THE SEASON

Harrison hasn't been the star the Cardinals, or anyone, expected outside since he was drafted. That's how a first-round investment turns into a second-round in-season trade 33 NFL games later.

Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. (18) runs a route against the Los Angeles Chargers during the second half of an NFL game at SoFi Stadium on Sept. 13, 2026, in Inglewood, Calif. (Cooper Neill/Getty Images)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

But the Texans obviously believe they can help Harrison meet their potential.

JADEVEON CLOWNEY'S CAREER FILLED WITH HIGH EXPECTATIONS IS NOW SUPPOSED TO DELIVER A HOUSTON TEXANS SUPER BOWL

Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud warms up before an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos Sunday, Nov. 2, 2025, in Houston. (AP Photo/Eric Christian Smith)

It is suddenly an optimistic time for the Texans. They are 1-4 and are buyers before the November trade deadline.

And Ryans told his players after Sunday's win, "let's go do something special."

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

articles.title: UK Greens leader seeks rule change after party declares Zionism is racism
articles.excerpt: Zack Polanski, the leader of the United Kingdom’s Green Party, has proposed a potential overhaul of his party’s democratic mechanisms, calling for the leader to have larger control over strategic dire...
articles.body_text:
Zack Polanski, the leader of the United Kingdom’s Green Party, has proposed a potential overhaul of his party’s democratic mechanisms, calling for the leader to have larger control over strategic direction.

The appeal came in an article published in The Guardian on Sunday after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference on October 4 in a divisive vote.

Polanski also failed to grab a parliamentary seat in the wake of the row with Israel in a by-election.

The Labour Party won the election for the parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer in Holborn and St Pancras on Friday, fending off a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he wrote.

“Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better,” the Green Party leader added.

Polanski also replied to the criticisms of him for not participating in the vote on the motion on Zionism.

“I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential by-election for our party,” he said, adding that he put all his “energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras”.

He admitted that some members feel “let down” by his decision not to make an appearance there.

The Green Party’s motion, which called for “Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party MPs.

After conceding defeat in the fiercely contested by-election, Polanski answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader.

He was barred from entering Israel after his party backed a motion to define Zionism as racism.

articles.title: Hidden clues could help predict a woman’s breast cancer risk years in advance
articles.excerpt: AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Br...
articles.body_text:
AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Breast Advice' Dr. Elisa Port highlights how AI uncovers hidden tumors and slashes false positive results, especially for women with dense breasts. This advancement aims to increase screening adherence among the 30-40% who currently don't get regular mammograms.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.

The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.

NEW ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TEST PREDICTS WHO IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP DEMENTIA IN 5 TO 10 YEARS

The model was developed using more than 313,000 mammograms from more than 161,000 women, according to the study.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance. (iStock)

Connie Lehman, a Massachusetts-based breast imaging specialist and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that AI could help identify women whose increased risk might otherwise go unnoticed.

"For decades, as a doctor and breast imaging specialist, I have cared for women who were shocked by a breast cancer diagnosis," Lehman said. "Again and again, I heard: 'How can this be? No one in my family has had breast cancer.'"

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues within a woman's breast tissue, according to Lehman.

The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time. (iStock)

"A mammogram can tell us more than whether cancer is visible today — it can also provide information about a woman's risk of developing cancer in the years ahead," she said.

That information could eventually help doctors tailor breast cancer screening to a woman's individual risk, Lehman said.

Women identified as being at increased risk could discuss additional screening, such as MRI, with their health care providers, while women at average risk may continue with routine mammograms, according to Lehman.

The technology could also analyze mammograms a woman has already had, meaning the added risk information would not require another imaging exam or additional radiation, she noted.

Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues in a woman's breast tissue, experts say. (iStock)

Lehman cautioned that an AI risk score is not a cancer diagnosis and cannot predict with certainty whether a woman will develop the disease.

"A higher score can prompt a conversation with your health care provider about additional screening and risk-reduction options," she said. "A lower score does not eliminate risk or replace regular mammography."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The NYU model remains a research tool and is not FDA-authorized for clinical use, according to Lehman.

The researchers also noted that more testing is needed. The study used mammograms from NYU Langone hospitals and imaging equipment from one manufacturer.

The team plans to test the model using data from other medical centers and different 3D mammography systems, according to NYU Langone.

Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.
