articles.title: Judge orders Tennessee to preserve all evidence from botched Christa Pike execution attempt – latest updates
articles.excerpt: Lawyer says Pike cannot move her arms or swallow, has a blot clot and pneumonia, adding that a request to unshackle her was refused; judge tells Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from botch...
articles.body_text:
Lawyer says Pike cannot move her arms or swallow, has a blot clot and pneumonia, adding that a request to unshackle her was refused; judge tells Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from botched execution

Christa Pike’s lawyer Randy Spivey added that she was “at peace” last Wednesday, adding: “She helped the execution team find what they thought was venous access. She was kind and polite as they worked for an hour, stabbing her arm with needle after needle, and then she felt the burn of the pentobarbital.”

Spivey added: “Our understanding was the first thing she said was ‘Where am I and who are you?’ There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people. She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.

“She is very aware that the state tried to execute her,” Spivey continued.

Explaining the steps ahead, Christa Pike’s lawyer said: “Until yesterday, Ms. Pike was unable to to speak. She was unconscious. She was not able to to authorize us to file any any sort of new lawsuits.”

“And so the motion that we filed is is just to preserve evidence. It’s it’s the very very first step of of what will be a long legal battle, we presume,” he added.

Christa Pike’s lawyer continued to describe her physical appearance following the botched execution attempt, saying: “I will say that like the swelling is what I noticed.”

“Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical [glove],” he added.

Christa Pike’s lawyer Randy Spivey added that she was “at peace” last Wednesday, adding: “She helped the execution team find what they thought was venous access. She was kind and polite as they worked for an hour, stabbing her arm with needle after needle, and then she felt the burn of the pentobarbital.”

Spivey added: “Our understanding was the first thing she said was ‘Where am I and who are you?’ There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people. She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.

“She is very aware that the state tried to execute her,” Spivey continued.

Christa Pike’s lawyers are providing more details on the state Pike has been in following the botched execution attempt.

“On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain dead, and that life support would be removed the next day. But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team, and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking,” her lawyer Randy Spivey said.

“Christa has a long road to recovery. She has a blood clot in one of her arms. She has pneumonia. She is not able to swallow yet, so she is not eaten. She cannot move either of her arms. Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms. But we do know that there’s a long road ahead, and that is just the physical toll that all of this is taking,” Spivey added.

Christa Pike’s lawyers are now holding a press conference following a court hearing at the Davidson county chancery court in Nashville, Tennessee.

“Today’s hearing was about transparency, about why Christa, the courts, the media, and the public should not simply take the state’s word about what happened last Wednesday, because as we saw a little bit today, their word is shrouded in secrecy, in legal jargons, in attempts to obfuscate and obscure what really happened,” Pike’s lawyer Luke Ihnen said.

Judge I’Ashea Myles has also said that “counsel are expected to follow all visitation policies that are in place at the respective hospital”.

She added: “This court will not run afoul of whatever the facility has already in place,” saying that “there is a two-hour response on whether or not visitation will be allowed”.

“If an incarcerated individual is allowed visitation once a day from counsel, the court does not expect TDOC to deviate from that simply because the petitioner is in a hospital facility versus a prison facility,” Myles added.

The judge says she is granting the motion to preserve all relevant evidence after telling the court: “This case is unique to say the least.”

I’Ashea Myles goes through a list of things Tennessee officials must preserve. It includes all drugs, IV lines and tubing that are in the state’s possession – “anything that was in the actual room” must be preserved and “that includes trash”.

Myles adds that anything that relates to the drug or supplies used must be preserved, as well as photographs, videos, audio recording, surveillance footage and anything in the witness rooms.

She also wants all communications, whether encrypted or not, to be preserved, stressing that this includes “anything concerning deviation from protocol or delays or equipment issues”.

She also warns: “Take special care not to lose, misplace, accidentally delete any information pertinent to this litigation.”

Assistant attorney general John W Ayers also pushed back against Christa Pike’s lawyers’ claims that their access to Pike is being limited by the Tennessee corrections department (TDOC).

He said: “TDOC does not intend to obstruct access to counsel. That’s why there’s been a process set up to request visitation to facilitate that. Now, these requests that were just layered on today go above and beyond what the conditions were before.”

Ayers said that Pike “never had unfettered access to a phone”, explaining that phone calls were arranged in advance but that Pike did have “unfettered access to a tablet”.

“Again, access to counsel is being facilitated. TDOC is not taking the position that counsel be should be excluded,” he said.

Evidence collected on 30 September by prison staff following the botched execution attempt on Christa Pike include observation logs, medical waste and products, as well as EKG readouts, assistant attorney general John W Ayers said.

He added that some evidence may not be in prison officials’ possession, saying: “It’s my understanding that the IV lines were cut, and so there may be portions of those IV lines that could have been still attached to Ms Pike when she was transported to the hospital.”

He added: “[The Tennessee correction department] can’t be ordered to preserve evidence that’s in the custody of another party, and so there may be items that were originally in TDOC’s custody that got transported to the hospital on the night of September 30. Again, counsel can confer on that and establish where that evidence is, but it would be premature and prejudicial, quite frankly, to enter an order requiring preservation of that kind of evidence before counsel had a chance to confer on it and get a picture of where that evidence might be.”

Christa Pike’s lawyers said that Pike remains shackled to her hospital bed.

“Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request by [the Tennessee corrections department],” they said, adding: “We would also amend our request and ask for that relief.”

Pike’s lawyers have also said that although they have been able to visit Pike since her botched execution attempt, “there are still obstacles being put in our way for that,” including waiting in a hospital lobby for over two hours before their visit request was approved.

Christa Pike’s lawyer tells the court that the state of Tennessee had made no promises that it will not seek a future execution.

“The state has made no promises that Ms Pike will not be subject to a future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes, because as we pled in January, the same thing is likely to happen,” Luke Ihnen said.

He argues that is a reason why records must be preserved as it is likely Pike will face a future execution attempt.

Ihnen accused officials of “secreting away” evidence.

Judge I’Ashea Myles said the state has agreed that the Davidson county court has the authority to hear the case. She will now officially reopen it.

Christa Pike’s lawyer, Luke Ihnen, is now going through the complaints her team has filed, pointing out issues in the botched execution protocol and the qualifications of prison staff.

“The new protocol allows for the placement of a ‘central line’. However, upon information and belief, the defendants do not have the medical personnel or equipment and cannot secure the same,” he said.

He also said: “Ms Pike has a history of difficulty with blood draws and needle insertion. Prison medical staff often use a butterfly needle on her arm to draw blood, because her veins are so difficult to access. The plaintiff’s physical characteristics will make it significantly more difficult to achieve and or maintain.”

One of Christa Pike’s lawyers, Luke Ihnen, said Pike was “speaking, limitedly” as he addressed Judge I’Ashea Myles about procedural issues in the case, including whether the Davidson county court has jurisdiction.

Meanwhile, John W Ayers, an assistant attorney general, called Pike’s survival from two lethal injections an “unusual, procedural position”.

The court hearing of Christa Pike is now under way.

Pike’s lawyers are addressing the court at the moment.

There will be a press conference after the hearing. The press conference had originally been expected for 12pm ET.

The press conference hosted by Christa Pike’s lawyers will begin momentarily.

Stay tuned as we bring you the latest updates.

Update: the press conference will be held after the court appearance has finished.

In the modern era of the US death penalty, Tennessee has never executed a person who was 18 at the time of their offence – the youngest was 23. Over the past 50 years, the state sent seven men who were 18 when they committed murder to death row, but in each case the sentence was vacated.

Tadryl Shipp, Christa Pike’s accomplice, held a fascination with satanic imagery. It was he who carved a pentagram in the victim’s chest, sending the local media into a frenzy. Yet because he was 17 at the time, he was barred from execution under Tennessee law; today he is serving a life sentence and had his first, unsuccessful, parole hearing in October 2025.

Had Pike been 10 months younger, she too would have been legally protected from the execution chamber. As time has passed, experts in children’s brains development have come to recognize that 18 is but an arbitrary line in the sand; adolescents – whatever their specific age – are susceptible to impulsive behavior.

And then there’s gender. Some argue that the gender of the 45 women who are now held on death rows across the US is irrelevant to their eligibility for the ultimate punishment. But in Pike’s case, it seems all too pertinent, given the agonizing litany of sexual and physical abuse she endured throughout her childhood.

She was subjected to a bewildering array of abuse, including multiple rapes by three separate men and beatings by numerous relatives.

Age. Gender. Abuse. The ingredients are all there, Pike’s legal team argues in the clemency petition for her crime, terrible though it was, to be recast in a different light.

Tennessee’s top prison official is resigning following Christa Pike’s botched execution attempt.

Over the weekend, governor Bill Lee announced that Frank Strada, the department of correction commissioner, will leave his position in late October amid an independent investigation into Pike’s failed execution attempt.

Despite calling the case “deeply disturbing,” Lee told reporters last week: “So far as we know, the department of correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined.” Meanwhile, Strada said that his resignation would “be in the best interests” of the state as the investigation goes underway.

Death penalty lawyers said that Strada oversaw five “botched” executions, with common threads including prolonged suffering among prisoners and questionable injection procedures.

On September 30, Christa Pike, who was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years, survived two doses of pentobarbital, a sedatative.

Witnesses to the attempt to execute Pike described how they heard she was choking and struggling for an hour after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her. In the hospital, she was put on a ventilator and had been in critical condition.

Speaking to the BBC, Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike’s team, said: “She has some memories of being in the hospital but no memory, I believe, of the execution attempt.”

Zivot added that Pike was able to remember her name but incorrectly guessed the current month as September.

Christa Pike’s lawyers are holding a press conference today after revealing last night that their client was “conscious and speaking” following last week’s botched execution attempt in Tennessee.

The 50-year old death row inmate is still receiving critical care in a hospital while “handcuffed and shackled to the bed”, her lawyers said on Tuesday, adding: “Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”

Speaking to the BBC, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike’s team said that she is able to communicate in a “basic way” but did not seem to remember last Wednesday’s execution attempt.

Her legal team will ask a court on at a hearing on Wednesday to require the Tennessee department of correction to preserve all “relevant physical, written and electronic evidence” related to the failed execution, court documents said.

The press conference is scheduled for noon ET.

Stay tuned as we bring you the latest live updates from the press conference.

articles.title: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan
articles.excerpt:
Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech

Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax...
articles.body_text:
Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech

Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.

The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England.

The move would mean the number of families paying inheritance tax – currently less than 5% do so – would fall by more than a half, Badenoch said, with the £6bn cost to be paid for by cuts the party says it has identified, including to the welfare bill.

“My ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it,” she told the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. “I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort. So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home, and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.”

The Tories’ policy plans announced this week – also including support with childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and repealing the mansion tax – have been firmly focused on affluent middle-class voters, many of whom deserted the party at the last election.

They have been welcomed by Conservative MPs and activists, who are relieved that Badenoch appears to be trying to shore up the party’s core support despite her natural proclivity to lean into culture wars on the right.

However, the inheritance tax plans are likely to raise fears about overheating the housing market, giving elderly homeowners an incentive to stay in large family homes rather than downsize. The move also prompted accusations the party was favouring the rich over struggling families.

In a statement, Tax Justice UK said: “Kemi Badenoch has just announced a massive inheritance tax giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Britain. This is a reckless policy that will deprive public services of cash when they most need them.”

Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes. These will mostly be people living in London and the south-east.”

Reform UK suggested Badenoch’s inheritance tax plans would only affect 2% of houses, the majority in London. Its finance spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, added: “The Tory party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country.”

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair and minister for equalities, said: “The Tories haven’t changed. Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories’ choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead.”

Despite the Tories appearing more united this week than they have done for years, Badenoch did acknowledge in her speech that the party, still polling lower than at the time of its catastrophic 2024 election defeat, faced a long path to recovery.

She issued an appeal to Reform voters to back her. “We let them down and we want them to come back home. They deserve better than Reform politicians,” she said. “We have changed our party. There is still a lot of work to do. People are looking through the shop window. They like what they see, but let’s be honest, not enough of them are buying it. We need to fix that.”

Senior Tories have been urging Badenoch to focus more on the economy, which they hope will help them to win back middle-class swing voters in their traditional heartlands, and to pivot away from culture wars and migration.

Badenoch added that economic growth would be the “central organising principle” of the next Conservative government, cutting red tape in areas such as planning, building a third runway at Heathrow and implementing a new energy policy, while also creating jobs.

Most of her speech, however, was devoted to attacks on her opponents, with the Tories desperate to edge ahead of Reform in the polls and be seen once again as the main opposition party on the right.

Badenoch rejected calls from within her own party to “unite the right” by striking a deal with Nigel Farage’s party – reflecting warnings from her closest allies that doing so would risk toxifying the Conservative brand irrevocably.

She said: “A year ago, those politicians were measuring up the curtains for No 10. Now, some of them are measuring up the curtains for their prison cells. 
 “The circus goes on and on, and it will never stop because this is who Reform politicians are. So, to those who say ‘unite the right’, we are not uniting with that. People deserve better and we are going to give them better than that: character, conduct and standards matter.”

Badenoch also drew a sharp dividing line with Reform on race, after Suella Braverman, the former Conservative home secretary who defected to Farage’s party, suggested that minority ethnic people could not be English.

“I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “I remember back in the day when Ian Wright and John Barnes were playing. Nobody was questioning whether they were English. We certainly didn’t have sitting MPs questioning whether they were English.

“We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are. Reform MPs are openly questioning people’s identity. I don’t know whether you’ve noticed, but I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country. I’m proud of our history, all that we have done, and all that we will do in the world.”

Badenoch acknowledged that last year her leadership of the party had been under intense pressure. But she added: “Let me tell you, I’m not someone who gets written off, and neither is the Conservative party. There is a reason our party is still here after 200 years. We have adapted to every single challenge and every single age, and we are doing it again.”

articles.title: Cost of Iran war explodes as toll on US air fleet nearly doubles
articles.excerpt:
Video from Iran shows US military aircraft appearing to conduct search for crew of downed F-15E Strike Eagle.

The U.S. military has lost or sustained damage to at least 81 aircraft during the war wit...
articles.body_text:
Video from Iran shows US military aircraft appearing to conduct search for crew of downed F-15E Strike Eagle.

The U.S. military has lost or sustained damage to at least 81 aircraft during the war with Iran — nearly double the number identified five months ago, according to a new government analysis that warns replacing some of the critical vehicles could strain the military's ability to meet demands elsewhere.

The aircraft include some of the military's most advanced fighters and critical support aircraft, as well as dozens of drones, the Congressional Research Service (CRS) noted in its report.

The tally is nearly double the 42 aircraft CRS identified in May as lost or damaged, although the increase partly reflects additional information becoming publicly available and does not mean all 39 additional aircraft were lost or damaged since that assessment.

ALARMING MISSILE REPORT DRAWS FORCEFUL RESPONSE FROM TRUMP AS IRAN WAR TESTS AMERICA’S ARSENAL

An F-15E Strike Eagle takes off for a combat flight in support of Operation Epic Fury during the Iran war at an undisclosed location on March 16, 2026. (U.S. Air Force/Reuters)

CRS, a nonpartisan arm of the Library of Congress that provides research and analysis to lawmakers and congressional committees, identified 12 F-15E Strike Eagles, an F-35A Lightning II, seven KC-135 refueling tankers, an E-3 Sentry airborne warning-and-control aircraft and 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones among those lost or damaged since Operation Epic Fury began on Feb. 28, 2026.

The body also warned that losses among aging, high-demand aircraft could create capability gaps or increase risk in other theaters, while production constraints and competing demands could affect how quickly the military rebuilds its capacity.

The 81 aircraft were lost or damaged through a mix of Iranian attacks, enemy fire, friendly fire, accidents and aircraft deliberately destroyed during rescue operations — though some damaged aircraft have since returned to service.

"We do not comment on reports from outside organizations or non-DOW battle damage assessments," a Department of War official told Fox News Digital when reached for comment on the report.

HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY

CRS cautioned that the tally could continue to change because of classification, ongoing combat operations and questions of attribution.

The new accounting comes more than eight months into a war that has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles and raised broader questions about how quickly the defense industrial base can replenish what the military is using. A Pentagon inspector general report last month found that the U.S. had spent an estimated $22.3 billion on munitions through June alone and warned of "strategic inventory shortfalls."

A US military MQ-9 Reaper drone approaches for landing at Rafael Hernandez Airport in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, on December 29, 2025. (Miguel J. Rodriguez Carrillo / AFP via Getty Images)

The Congressional Budget Office estimated in September that replacing equipment lost through Aug. 1 could cost between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on the Department of War's replacement plans.

Drones account for more than half of the aircraft in the new tally. At least 45 MQ-9 Reapers have been lost in operations against Iran, according to CRS, along with three MQ-1 drones and an MQ-4C Triton.

But while drones drive much of the raw number, the report also points to losses and damage among scarcer, harder-to-replace aircraft.

An E-3 Sentry was damaged in an Iranian attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia in March and was later reported to have sustained a "direct hit." CRS specifically flagged the aging and limited E-3 fleet as an example of how losses among high-demand aircraft could create capability gaps or increase risks for U.S. forces in other theaters.

Iranian attacks have also inflicted damage on U.S. aircraft while they were on the ground at bases across the region. Five KC-135 tankers were reportedly damaged at Prince Sultan Air Base in March, while eight F-15Es sustained light damage during an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan in September. The eight fighters were returned to service.

At least 18 U.S. service members have also died since the war began, though the Pentagon has divided those deaths between Operation Epic Fury and a separate category for the renewed fighting that began in July.

PENTAGON RACES TO BUY 10X MORE MISSILES AS IRAN WAR DWINDLES ARSENAL, THREATENS READINESS FOR CHINA AGGRESSION

This image from video provided by U.S. Central Command shows a missile being launched from a U.S. Navy ship in support of Operation Epic Fury on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026. (U.S. Central Command via AP)

Other losses illustrate the dangers surrounding recovery operations. Two MC-130J Commando II special operations aircraft were intentionally destroyed while supporting efforts to rescue the crew of a downed F-15E, while an HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopter was damaged during the same rescue effort. Four AH-6 Little Bird helicopters were later destroyed by U.S. forces during separate rescue operations, according to the Defense Department inspector general.

Three F-15Es were destroyed by friendly fire over Kuwait in the opening days of the war, while an F-35A was later damaged by Iranian ground fire over Iran.

CRS said the losses could prompt Congress to examine whether the U.S. industrial base can replace aircraft quickly enough to meet military requirements. The report also pointed to a broader operational question: whether the losses reflect changes in Iran's capabilities that require the U.S. to adjust its equipment, tactics or basing posture.

articles.title: Former CIA officer warns against trusting Russia's account of mysterious death in Siberia
articles.excerpt: Glenn Corn, who spent over 20 years in U.S. intelligence, says Russia's history of deception warrants skepticism as questions remain over the pneumonia death of a 28-year-old researcher who worked at ...
articles.body_text:
Glenn Corn, who spent over 20 years in U.S. intelligence, says Russia's history of deception warrants skepticism as questions remain over the pneumonia death of a 28-year-old researcher who worked at a lab with deadly pathogens.

Glenn Corn, a former CIA officer, told Fox News Digital that Russia’s decades-long history of deception makes it difficult to trust the Kremlin’s account of a possible disease outbreak following the death of a 28-year-old researcher at a facility containing dangerous pathogens.

Darya Shipilova, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, got sick near the end of September.

After unconfirmed reports that Shipilova died from pneumonic plague were shared far and wide on social media, Russian authorities pushed back, saying she died on Oct. 2 from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing found no evidence she had been infected with a pathogen from her lab.

Yet the Russian government’s past messaging around major crises has left Corn and others wary of its official account.

Glenn Corn attends the discussion organized by the Kyiv Security Forum in Kyiv, Ukraine, on April 3, 2026. (Yuliia Ovsiannikova/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS

"This is what the challenge is, because they have the history of the 'boy who cried wolf syndrome.' They have this history of being deceitful. It's very hard to believe what they're saying," Corn said.

Corn, who is fluent in Russian and spent more than 20 years overseas during his intelligence career, gave several examples of elaborate Russian coverups, including the 1979 anthrax outbreak that killed at least 64 people in the Soviet city of Sverdlovsk, now called Yekaterinburg.

For years, the Soviet Union claimed that the deaths were caused by intestinal anthrax from tainted meat, according to PBS Frontline. It wasn't until 1992 that President Boris Yeltsin finally admitted the illnesses were the result of military activity at a nearby biological weapons facility.

This dedication to deception, Corn said, remains a feature of the current government under President Vladimir Putin.

Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died after developing pneumonia of an unknown cause, prompting quarantines and heightened health precautions in the region. Russian authorities say testing has found no evidence her illness was linked to pathogens she worked with. (East2West news)

AMB. GORDON SONDLAND: THE GODFATHER TEST -- HOW PUTIN TURNS EVERY ATTACK INTO A MYSTERY—AND GETS AWAY WITH IT

Corn pointed to the Kremlin’s past denials of ties to the Wagner mercenary group, whose murky relationship with the state allowed its fighters to advance Moscow’s interests overseas while Russian officials maintained plausible deniability. Putin later acknowledged that the group had been fully financed by the Russian state.

"This goes to the strategic culture of leadership in Russia...and their fear of the rest of the world, and their belief that they have to deceive everybody because everybody is deceiving them," Corn said.

Corn said this style of narrative control is also characteristic of China, which remains under Communist Party rule, while modern Russia inherited many of the institutions and governing practices of the communist-led Soviet Union.

For example, China faced criticism in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic for withholding or delaying the release of critical information about the emerging virus, which has gone on to kill more than 7 million people globally.

Workers in protective uniforms conduct testing in Russia amid heightened precautions following the death of an employee at a Siberian anti-plague research institute. (Khuvsguliinungu.mn/e2w)

TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

"In both systems, people are disincentivized to tell the truth when there's a bad story," Corn said. "Nobody wants to actually say that we have a real problem and we need to deal with it because they're afraid that it will cost them their jobs, their lives, their freedom."

With that history in mind, Corn said U.S. officials should not simply take Moscow at its word on Shipilova’s death, but independently verify its claims and closely monitor for any signs of a wider outbreak.

So far, there is no sign that Shipilova’s illness has spread. Russia's health watchdog said Tuesday that 60% of the roughly 200 people quarantined after potentially coming in contact with Shipilova have been released. It added that no cases of plague have been found.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a Security Council meeting via videolink in Moscow on Oct. 7, 2026. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Pool / AFP via Getty Images)

The World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday that the case presented a "very low" risk outside Russia, The Associated Press reported.

That same day, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on social media that the global health agency is in contact with Russian health authorities and has requested more information "to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia" that killed Shipilova.

President Donald Trump also told reporters on Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Putin about the case "very soon," adding that the U.S. is already in "very deep discussions" with Russia.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

articles.title: British Jewish groups hold London vigil for victims of 7 October attacks
articles.excerpt:
Organisations honour those who died three years ago as prime minister says government ‘stands with’ British Jews

British Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honou...
articles.body_text:
Organisations honour those who died three years ago as prime minister says government ‘stands with’ British Jews

British Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks in Israel, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.

The vigil took place at Richmond Terrace, opposite Downing Street.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Three years ago, Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel, murdering 1,200 men, women and children, injuring thousands and taking 251 people captive. May their memories for ever remain a blessing.”

Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council said 7 October had been “the deadliest day for our people since the Holocaust”.

The attacks were followed by Israel’s war in Gaza. The Palestinian death toll in the past three years exceeded 74,000 last month, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is part of the Hamas-led government.

Andy Burnham assured British Jews “we stand with you” against antisemitism, in a statement marking the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks.

However, the Israeli embassy said in a statement: “It is a source of deep sadness that, in the years since 7 October, the position of the British government towards Israel has changed so substantially from the solidarity expressed in those first days,” claiming “the atmosphere for Jewish people continues to worsen” in the UK.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine last month.

The Community Security Trust (CST), which monitors antisemitism, said its research showed there were 1,926 antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK from January to June 2026, up by a fifth on the first half of last year and the second-highest total reported to the CST in the first six months of any year.

It was exceeded only by the 2,019 incidents recorded in the first half of 2024, which followed the 2023 Hamas attacks and the start of Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza.

Celebrations of Jewish life have been continuing in public spaces. From 27 September to 2 October, the Jewish festival of Sukkot was celebrated in the heart of Manchester, with the Sukkah in the City event in Albert Square.

In his statement, the prime minister described the rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK since 2023 as “disturbing”, but pledged his government was “committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred”.

Burnham referenced an attack just over a year ago on the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur by Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Manchester, which left two worshippers dead.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from stab wounds and his fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors from Al-Shamie. Police shot Al-Shamie dead during the attack.

Burnham said: “Three years on from the 7 October attacks on Israel, we remember those who were senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists.

“The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day.

“In the years since, we have seen a disturbing rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK.

“I want Britain’s Jewish community to hear this from me directly: we stand with you. Abuse and violence against you, in any form, will not be tolerated. Not on our streets, not online, not in our schools or universities.

“That’s why we are funding protection for synagogues, schools and community buildings, and why we will come down hard on antisemitism wherever it is found – in classrooms, on campuses and in neighbourhoods.

“At home, we are committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred. Abroad, we continue to work towards a two-state solution, with Israelis and Palestinians living side-by-side in peace and security.

“An attack on Jewish people in Britain is an attack on all of us. Antisemitism has no place in this country, and we will do everything we can to stamp it out.”

Meanwhile, the Metropolitan police said it had “imposed stringent conditions” on those taking part in a pro-Palestine student march in London on Wednesday.

Eleven people were arrested in the capital, including five on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London, the force said.

The Met said the other arrests were made at pro-Palestinian student protests elsewhere in London.

Pro-Palestine protesters also held demonstrations at Edinburgh and Glasgow universities.

Hundreds of people gathered for a rally outside George Square in Edinburgh, outside the University of Edinburgh’s Main Library.

From there they marched to the Bayes Centre – the university’s hub for data science and artificial intelligence – before finishing in the Old College quadrangle.

A similar demonstration was held on Library Hill in Glasgow, outside the university library.

Protesters at both rallies carried Palestinian flags and banners, many bearing slogans about the conflict in Gaza.

After testifying before Congress, McEnroe explains why he believes this issue is even more widespread than the debate over transgender athletes in women’s sports—and why lawmakers need to act. He also weighs in on the changing culture of the US Open and the future of college athletics.

Days after finding herself in the midst of an on-court controversy, followed by responding to a racial slur on social media, Coco Gauff was eliminated in the round of 16 of the China Open.

Gauff dropped her Wednesday match to No. 19 Elise Mertens 6-3, 6-3, and in the midst of the match, she admitted to not being in the right state.

"I have no energy. I’m trying, I have no energy. I can’t see the ball, I feel like I’m going to pass out," Gauff told her camp during the match, according to the New York Post. "I’m going to just try to finish the match."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Coco Gauff of the United States walks off the court after losing to Elise Mertens of Belgium in the fourth round on Day 8 of the China Open at National Tennis Center on Oct. 7, 2026 in Beijing, China. (Robert Prange/Getty Images)

After the match, Gauff said the aftermath of what had happened earlier in the week had "been kind of draining."

"I'm not going to lie," she said. "I just turn off my phone and move on. There's nothing you can do."

The defeat to a player Gauff had beaten in all five of their previous matchups came days after she had received what she described as an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in the preceding round.

Gauff stopped a rally after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Xinran, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title. Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing, but the chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.

Gauff explained what occurred in the moment, but not before replying to a post on X calling her a racial slur.

Coco Gauff of the United States celebrates after defeating Xinran Sun of China in a Women's Singles Round of 32 match on day six of the China Open at the National Tennis Center in Beijing, China, on Oct. 5, 2026. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)

PATRICK MCENROE ON U.S. OPEN WEED SMELL, TRANS ATHLETES, FOREIGN RECRUITS RESHAPING COLLEGE TENNIS

"hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist. the amount of racist comments/dms I’ve received in the last few hours is insane," Gauff said, adding that she is "not a cheater or a thief."

"It was an unfortunate situation but it is out of my control, the think pieces and calling me an unfair is ridiculous when those are the rules. I did not make them, I think it’s weird i’m getting hate for following the rules," Gauff said in a separate social media post. "Xinran is incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood."

Coco Gauff of the United States reacts against Xinran Sun of China in the women's singles third round match at the China Open in Beijing on Oct. 5, 2026. (Lintao Zhang/Getty Images)

Against Mertens, Gauff committed 34 unforced errors to Mertens’ 11 and had eight double faults to her opponent’s two. Four of Gauff’s double faults came when she was broken in the final game of the first set.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Israel amb torches Mamdani Oct 7 post: 'Like turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda'
articles.excerpt: Nova Music Festival survivor Natalie Sanandaji and Holocaust survivor Sami Steigmann join ‘America’s Newsroom’ on the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks. Sanandaji recounts her fight for survi...
articles.body_text:
Nova Music Festival survivor Natalie Sanandaji and Holocaust survivor Sami Steigmann join ‘America’s Newsroom’ on the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks. Sanandaji recounts her fight for survival, while Steigmann warns about rising antisemitism around the world.

Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations blasted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his message marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks, comparing the mayor’s framing of the massacre to "turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists."

Ambassador Danny Danon accused Mamdani of trying to "hijack" the anniversary after the mayor commemorated the more than 1,100 Israelis killed by Hamas before pivoting to accusations of "genocide," "occupation" and "apartheid" against Israel.

"‘Mamdani-ism’ — an attempt to hijack the anniversary of October 7 and turn it into yet another propaganda attack against Israel," Danon wrote on X in response to the mayor’s post.

MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'

Israel's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Danny Danon condemned New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani for using a message on the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attack to make accusations against Israel. (Reuters/David Dee Delgado)

"It is like turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists," he added. "We will not let this happen. We will remember those who were murdered, and we will never forget who was behind this massacre."

Mamdani’s post Wednesday began by calling the anniversary "profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers" and describing the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack as "horrific war crimes."

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani smiles in reaction to reporters' comments after a private meeting with President Donald Trump at Gracie Mansion on Manhattan's Upper East Side, New York, N.Y., Sept. 21, 2026. (Anthony Behar/Sipa USA)

"On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others," Mamdani wrote. "We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."

DANNY DANON: FROM OCT 7 TO FLIGHT 1073: THE RESILIENCE THAT KEEPS ISRAEL STANDING

The mayor then turned much of his statement toward the war in Gaza, accusing the Israeli government of carrying out a "devastating, ongoing genocide" and citing a Palestinian death toll of more than 74,000, including more than 21,000 children.

"The suffering did not begin nor end that day," Mamdani wrote.

Mamdani accused Israel of bombing ambulances, targeting residential buildings and journalists with drone strikes and turning away food aid at border crossings. Israel has disputed allegations that it deliberately targets civilians, aid workers and journalists and has rejected accusations of genocide, noting flyers that the Israeli military has sent to Palestinian civilians warning them of attacks in advance and urging them to get to safety.

The mayor also accused the U.S. government of complicity in Israeli "war crimes" through its military support.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a press conference during moving day at Gracie Mansion on Jan. 12, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment," Mamdani wrote. "To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity."

MAMDANI FIRES BACK AT NETANYAHU, CALLS ISRAELI LEADER 'ARCHITECT OF HORRIFIC GENOCIDE' AHEAD OF UN VISIT

Danon was not alone in objecting to Mamdani’s framing of the anniversary.

"Disgusting and shameful to use October 7th as an excuse to repeat Hamas’ talking points. The terrorist enemies that seek to destroy us will not prevail. We stand with the Jewish people and we pray for the victims, their families and the survivors," said Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.

"Shame on you for trying to blow a kiss and slap Israelis in the face at the same time," posted former U.S. Ambassador to the UN Nikki Haley. "On October 7, Hamas raped, burned, and murdered Israelis and Americans in front of their loved ones. They kidnapped others and tortured them for months. This is antisemitism, no matter how you try to put a bow on it. Israelis have every right to defend themselves. If this happened in the U.S., you can bet we would defend ourselves too."

".@NYCMayor , not once do you say 'Jews.' On Oct. 7, Hamas-led attackers murdered civilians, committed sexual violence, mutilated bodies and took hostages," said Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt. "You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points. The city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel deserves a mayor who can honor the dead without exploiting them."

Hamas-led terrorists stormed southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing roughly 1,200 people in brutal fashion while livestreaming the atrocities online, and taking 251 hostages. Israelis marked the third anniversary Wednesday with memorials and vigils for those killed and abducted.

articles.title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
articles.excerpt:
Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the decision to pause the expansion was a difficult one

Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sol...
articles.body_text:
Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the decision to pause the expansion was a difficult one

Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.

It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.

On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".

Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare.

A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.

Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.

Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.

The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.

That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so.

However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.

Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.

"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.

Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.

Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid.

Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.

Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.

But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.

"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.

Canada should 'indefinitely exclude' people with mental illness from assisted dying, report says

What is a 'safe death'? Mentally ill woman asks for assisted dying in Canada

'I could live 30 years but plan to die': How assisted dying law is dividing Canadians

Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death".

Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that the government's decision is "deeply disappointing".

"People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said.

More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort.

In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying.

It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services".

The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium.

Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased".

Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access, external to medically assisted death but that support falls it comes to patients with mental illness alone.

Watch: One mentally ill man's fight for assisted dying in Canada

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

articles.title: Over 100 arrested in Belgium student protests over education costs
articles.excerpt: Police in Belgium have detained more than 100 people after demonstrations in the city of Liege against the rising cost of education turned violent in some places, as similar protests grip neighbouring...
articles.body_text:
Police in Belgium have detained more than 100 people after demonstrations in the city of Liege against the rising cost of education turned violent in some places, as similar protests grip neighbouring France.

Students rallied in the city on Tuesday and Wednesday against overcrowded classrooms and difficulty accessing resources in Belgium’s French-language education system.

Eighty people were detained during the protests, and 27 were formally arrested, the Belga news agency reported, citing the Liege police.

Some protesters damaged property and set fires, the police added.

Attendees insisted that shortcomings in the education system gave them no choice but to take to the streets.

“When we saw nothing was changing without protests, we decided we would start,” said Amelia Di Salve, a 19-year-old studying to become a teacher, who added that protests in “France did influence us a little”.

“We support each other because we’re facing pretty much the same issues,” Alfred, another 19-year-old ⁠student, told the Reuters news agency.

Authorities were attempting to defuse tensions and head off further unrest.

“Dialogue can be established,” Willy Demeyer, the mayor of the city of Liege, told Belgian broadcaster RTBF, adding that he hoped “young people can express their grievances in a peaceful way and if possible have those concerns heard”.

In Belgium, education is managed independently by the country’s linguistic communities, and there is no single national curriculum.

Instead, the Flemish population regulates education in Belgium’s Dutch-speaking Flanders region while French-speaking Wallonia oversees its own curriculum.

Parents can decide where to enrol children in the bilingual capital Brussels.

The protests in Liege follow sporadic violent demonstrations over the summer in Brussels against an increase in tuition fees for students in French-speaking areas from 835 euros ($930) to 1,194 euros ($1,340).

Belgium’s education budget has been under pressure as a result of a cost-of-living crisis and the spiralling cost of energy, issues that are helping fuel student protests in France as well.

Fox News correspondent Mark Meredith reports on how remote work is reshaping office spaces and transforming the workplace 30 years after Fox News launched on ‘America Reports.’

Nineteen years ago today, I walked through the doors at 1211 and hit the ground running — covering some of the biggest stories of our lifetimes, from the 2008 financial crisis to presidential elections that reshaped the country.

What followed has been an intense, exciting and incredibly rewarding career at Fox News.

I’ve had the privilege of moderating presidential primary debates, conducting the first live interview inside the Vice President’s Ceremonial Office, interviewing Supreme Court justices, presidents, military leaders and Wall Street CEOs, and reporting live from the trading floors of New York and Chicago.

LAUREN GREEN: I WAS FOX NEWS CHANNEL'S FIRST ON-AIR HIRE. HERE'S HOW A DREAM BECAME A POWERHOUSE

I’ve also been fortunate to help launch some great shows — "Outnumbered" in 2014, the relaunch of "America’s Newsroom" in 2018, and "America Reports with John Roberts and Sandra Smith" in 2021.

Today, those shows are a driving force behind Fox News’ No. 1 position in daytime — a testament to the extraordinary teams that show up every day ready to fight for the story.

And somewhere along the way, I took on my most important role of all: becoming a mom, twice. Balancing motherhood and this career has taught me more about discipline, sacrifice and perspective than anything else ever could.

DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE

But after 19 years, it’s not the stories or the interviews that stand out most.

Fox has become a second family. I’m incredibly grateful to Lachlan, Suzanne and Jay for their leadership and for continuing to give me the opportunity to grow, take on new challenges and do work that I genuinely love.

FOX NEWS MEDIA CEO SUZANNE SCOTT INDUCTED INTO BROADCASTING+CABLE HALL OF FAME

Sandra Smith attends the 2026 White House Correspondents' Dinner at Washington Hilton on April 25, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)

And after all these years, what drives me is still the same thing that drove me on day one: the viewers. They deserve someone who is prepared, asks the hard questions and never stops working for them.

Nineteen years in, I’m still here. Still fighting for the story. Still loving the work.

And I’m more excited than ever for what comes next.

articles.title: Grocery shoppers may be relying on a 'misleading' clue when choosing healthy foods
articles.excerpt: Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder of Kelly’s Choice, discusses new research showing that consumers often view foods with shorter shelf lives as healthier, even when tha...
articles.body_text:
Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder of Kelly’s Choice, discusses new research showing that consumers often view foods with shorter shelf lives as healthier, even when that isn’t necessarily the case.

A shorter shelf life may make food seem fresher and healthier, but new research suggests that may be more perception than reality.

A study from the University of British Columbia (UBC) Sauder School of Business in Canada found that many shoppers use a food's shelf life as a shortcut for judging how natural it is, even though longer shelf lives can reflect factors beyond heavy processing.

The team, which included researchers from China, conducted a series of experiments in which participants compared foods with different shelf lives, including potato chips, pasta sauce, mayonnaise and granola bars.

YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS

Shoppers consistently viewed foods with shorter shelf lives as more natural and healthier, even when the ingredients and nutritional facts were nearly identical or the difference in shelf life was solely due to better packaging.

Packaged foods with longer shelf lives may be perceived as less natural, even when the difference is simply better packaging, new research found. (iStock)

In the case of the mayonnaise, the only difference between the two products was that one had a better seal, allowing it to stay fresh longer — it was no more processed than the other. Yet participants still viewed the shorter-shelf-life option as more natural.

Even when they were given clear indications that a longer-lasting product just had better packaging, shoppers still used shelf life as a gauge, the researchers found.

JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

In other experiments, participants rated potato chips with a five-month shelf life as more natural and healthier than nearly identical chips with a nine-month shelf life.

Products such as mayonnaise might last longer simply because of improved packaging, not because they contain more preservatives. (iStock)

Nearly 70% of participants selected a pasta sauce with a one-year shelf life when they were encouraged to prioritize natural foods.

That figure dropped to 43% when the emphasis shifted to reducing food waste and protecting the environment, as the researchers found that participants also associated longer shelf life with less waste because items wouldn't go bad as quickly.

The findings, published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology earlier this year, suggest shoppers often use shelf life as a "mental shortcut" when making purchasing decisions, researchers said.

AMERICANS ARE DITCHING ULTRA-PROCESSED SNACKS FOR AN ANCIENT FRUIT THAT'S EXPLODING IN POPULARITY

"Our research shows consumers are using shelf life as a shortcut for judging whether foods are natural," co-author Yann Cornil, an associate professor at UBC Sauder, told Fox News Digital.

"It sometimes can be diagnostic, but shelf life is also very much dependent on the quality of the packaging, which has nothing to do with food naturalness."

Better seals and moisture-controlled packaging can extend a food's freshness without adding preservatives. (iStock)

Cornil added that the shortcut can be "misleading."

THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW

Packaging has improved dramatically, he noted, just like refrigeration did 60 years ago, to improve food preservation.

The tendency to equate a shorter shelf life with less processing may have unintended consequences, according to the researchers. Buyers may therefore skip products that are just as healthy while choosing items that are more likely to spoil before they can be eaten.

Products like canned beans, frozen fruits and vegetables and dried oats can stay fresh for months or even years thanks to preservation methods and packaging rather than added ingredients.

"A shorter shelf life does not automatically mean a food is healthier," Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder and CEO of Kelly's Choice, told Fox News Digital. "Better seals, oxygen barriers and moisture-control packaging help foods stay fresh longer while maintaining quality and safety."

Products with longer shelf lives may still be healthy choices, as packaging and preservation methods can help foods stay fresh longer. (iStock)

Springer pointed to some packaged items such as guacamole, which can have a longer refrigerated shelf life because of high-pressure processing and packaging technology rather than added preservatives, yet are still healthy choices.

Other items such as milk, yogurt and kefir can stay fresh longer due to pasteurization and fermentation — not necessarily added ingredients.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Don't judge a food by its shelf life," Springer, who was not involved in the research, added. "Turn the package over, read the nutrition label and make decisions based on what's inside."

Dairy products such as milk, yogurt and kefir can stay fresh longer because of pasteurization and fermentation. (iStock)

She recommends consumers focus on fiber, protein, added sugar and sodium rather than the expiration date alone.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Cornil added that saturated fat content can also be problematic.

"Too many ingredients, in particular ingredients [such as] additives and preservatives that you can't recognize, or can't even pronounce, may be a signal of too much processing and unhealthiness," Cornil said. "It's not always true, but I would say that it is more diagnostic than shelf life information."

The findings are especially relevant as many seek to reduce how much ultra-processed food they eat. Roughly 55% of Americans' daily caloric intake is from ultra-processed foods, the researchers noted.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
articles.excerpt:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk

US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of...
articles.body_text:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk

US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.

"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday.

In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled, and Russia's reporting of the death to the World Health Organization (WHO) was in line with standard practice. He accused the media of reporting "false information".

The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.

Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death. They say that those who came into contact with the victim all tested negative and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.

Earlier, the head of the WHO called for transparency from Russia.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.

contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials

Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.

Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.

The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.

Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.

But Russian officials have played down those reports. The country's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology".

Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.

The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.

It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death.

It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?

articles.title: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
articles.excerpt:
The winners are awarded the Nobel Prize medal and a share of 12.0 million Swedish Kroner ($1.25m; £900,000)

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan'...
articles.body_text:
The winners are awarded the Nobel Prize medal and a share of 12.0 million Swedish Kroner ($1.25m; £900,000)

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.

The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.

For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.

But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.

In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.

You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.

And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.

When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.

So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.

Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."

The chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, Heiner Linke, explains how chiral molecules have mirror forms like our hands

By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.

Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.

"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.

Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature, external describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.

In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.

"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".

At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.

Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".

"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.

President Donald Trump spent some time with a handful of Baltimore Ravens players on Tuesday during his event at Tradepoint Atlantic, where he touted the site for Anduril Industries' $3.7 billion "Arsenal-2" high-tech shipyard to manufacture submarine components.

During his remarks on the billion-dollar project at the 3,300-acre multimodal industrial and global logistics center located at Sparrows Point in Baltimore County, Maryland, Trump singled out four Ravens players in the audience on their day off.

Four-time Pro Bowl cornerback Marlon Humphrey, kicker Tyler Loop, long snapper Nick Moore and punter Ryan Eckley put on suits to attend the event and met with Trump.

(Getty Images)

TRUMP TURNS TO EMERGING TECH GIANT IN MULTI-BILLION BID TO RAMP UP US SUBMARINE PRODUCTION

And the president, who is probably the most sports-minded man to ever serve in the Oval Office, pointed them all out and gave the Ravens a shoutout.

"What a team you have this year," Trump said. "What a great team."

The Ravens have a 3-1 record and lead the AFC North division.

Trump met all the players prior to his remarks and then singled them out in front of the assembled audience and media.

"Could you stand up?" Trump asked the players. "You guys are where are you? Big stars. Where are you guys? There they are. Good looking guys."

"I said, tell me, are you a coach? They said, 'No, he's a snapper,'" Trump said. "You know, nowadays, those long snappers are very valuable. It's an amazing job you do with that. And he's got an unblemished record.

"How far is that, like, 10 yards deep or more? Fifteen yards and you throw strikes, you throw strikes. I don't know how to hell you do it. So, he's got a little gray hair right now, this, but you know, they don't care. They want them him for one play."

Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson, the team's biggest star, was not present at Tuesday's event. He is nursing an ankle injury and his status for Sunday's game against the Atlanta Falcons is uncertain.
